3	
4	The oracle experiments (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}, bottom) constitute causal interventions that isolate the source of failure. By replacing only the constraint source while holding all other pipeline components fixed, we establish that aggregation is not the bottleneck: the $+8.82$\,pp improvement on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$) pinpoint same-model self-extraction as the single point of failure. This oracle design follows established methodology where component-level interventions isolate error sources \citep{press2023compositionality, trivedi2023ircot, saparov2023greedy}.
5	
6	Constraint quality analysis on the full Qwen2.5-14B dataset (804 problems, 307 with multiple candidates, 7{,}844 unique constraints) explains the mechanism through two complementary metrics. \emph{Source-trace discriminativeness} measures whether a constraint's weight is concentrated on traces producing a single answer: 39.2\% of constraint weight is source-discriminative (95\% CI [38.7, 39.8]). \emph{Z3 semantic discriminativeness} asks whether a constraint can evaluate differently across candidates under Z3: only 8.2\% of constraints are semantically discriminative (95\% CI [7.6, 8.8]). The gap between these rates reveals the mechanism: constraints are statistically correlated with their source answers (39.2\%) but semantically equivalent across all candidates (91.8\%). Domain constraints encode shared facts (predicate definitions, background implications, intermediate steps) that Z3 satisfies identically regardless of the answer; only answer-assertion constraints carry semantic discriminative power. This structural analysis confirms that switching the scoring mechanism from source-trace attribution to direct Z3 evaluation would not change the outcome. The 803/804 agreement between MAX-SAT and count-only (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}) provides independent empirical confirmation.
7	
8	The computational cost is substantial: constraint extraction accounts for 48.7\% of total SICA pipeline time (measured on Qwen2.5-14B, FOLIO + ProofWriter combined, $n = 804$, single A6000 GPU), roughly doubling wall-clock cost compared to SC alone. SICA and SC disagree on 31 of 804 problems (3.9\%), but these disagreements approximately cancel: 16 SICA wins, 14 SC wins, and 1 both-wrong with different answers, yielding a net gain of only $+$2 problems (Appendix~\ref{app:case-studies} provides representative case studies). Bootstrap confidence intervals bound the true effect to [$-1.12$, $+1.62$]\,pp for the largest confirmatory condition ($n = 804$; Appendix Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap}): even if a small effect exists, it cannot justify the pipeline's additional complexity and cost.
9	
10	The oracle ceilings ($+8.82$\,pp on FOLIO, $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter) quantify the potential locked behind the capability trap, with larger gains on harder relational reasoning subtypes (RelNeg $+17.86$\,pp). The oracle gap suggests that constraint quality, not the extraction prompt format, is the primary bottleneck, though alternative extraction strategies (e.g., few-shot examples, iterative refinement, structured decomposition) were not tested in this study. Three concrete paths can unlock the potential. First, trained FOL extractors supervised on datasets with gold annotations (such as FOLIO) can learn extraction patterns that exceed same-model capabilities; FoVer \citep{wang2025fover} demonstrates this approach with a dedicated verifier. Second, external provers that verify constraints independently of the reasoning model eliminate the circular dependency between generation and verification. Third, cross-model extraction was tested directly: Mistral-7B extracting from Qwen2.5-14B traces yields $\Delta = 0.00$\,pp with 0\% discriminative rate (\S\ref{sec:interventions}), suggesting the extraction bottleneck is not model-specific but inherent to LLM constraint extraction from CoT traces. 11	
12	For practitioners considering constraint-based voting, $C_0$ provides a zero-cost screening criterion computable from the trace sampling stage alone, before any constraint extraction or solver invocation. When $C_0$ falls below 5\%, SICA degenerates to SC by construction. High $C_0$ is necessary but not sufficient, as the capability trap renders constraints non-discriminative even when disagreement is abundant ($C_0 = 61.8\%$, $\Delta = -2.45$~pp, n.s., for LLaMA-3.1-8B on FOLIO). The recommended workflow is: compute $C_0$, and if it exceeds 5\%, assess constraint quality on a small pilot before committing to full-scale extraction. More broadly, the evaluation framework developed here (oracle component isolation, dual discriminativeness metrics, and $C_0$ screening) applies to any pipeline where an LLM extracts formal structure from its own outputs. This reusable methodology can diagnose self-extraction bottlenecks beyond the SICA setting.
13	
14	\paragraph{Implications for Test-Time Scaling.}
15	Scaling test-time computation through additional reasoning traces faces diminishing returns under majority voting \citep{snell2025scaling, loo2025reevaluating}. Our oracle results demonstrate that symbolic verification can break this plateau: gold FOL constraints yield $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter, extracting substantial signal from the same traces that majority voting cannot use. The bottleneck is not the verification mechanism but the constraint source. Self-extracted constraints inherit the correlated errors of the traces they were derived from, producing what \citet{kambhampati2024position} term ``fake verification'' where the verifier cannot catch errors the generator makes. Z3 Feedback Refinement (\S\ref{sec:z3-feedback}) represents one attempt to break this circularity through the LLM-Modulo paradigm, where an external solver provides corrective signals that the model cannot generate through introspection. Whether this partial external grounding suffices to improve constraint discriminativeness remains an open empirical question (\S\ref{sec:diagnostics}). For practitioners, $C_0$ offers a zero-cost signal for whether test-time scaling has reached the majority-voting ceiling: when $C_0 < 5\%$, additional traces provide no new information, and investing in verification infrastructure rather than more samples becomes the rational allocation of test-time compute.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Scaling test-time computation has emerged as a key strategy for improving large language model (LLM) reasoning \citep{snell2025scaling}. Majority voting over multiple chain-of-thought samples, known as Self-Consistency (SC) \citep{wang2023sc}, remains the dominant aggregation method but faces diminishing returns from additional traces \citep{loo2025reevaluating}. Verification-based approaches that extract richer signal from reasoning traces offer a path to break this plateau. Symbolic verification through formal constraints and satisfiability solvers is one such direction, as it provides logical guarantees that natural language self-critique lacks \citep{huang2024selfcorrect}.

Neuro-symbolic methods that augment LLM reasoning with formal solvers have demonstrated gains on logical reasoning benchmarks. Logic-LM \citep{pan2023logiclm} and LINC \citep{olausson2023linc} delegate formalization to external provers. More recent systems route problems to specialized solver paradigms \citep{xu2026dylos}, apply logic-complete decomposition \citep{li2025aristotle}, train dedicated first-order logic (FOL) verifiers on supervised data \citep{wang2025fover}, or employ multi-perspective grounding \citep{luo2025logicagent}. These systems report positive results, but each introduces capabilities beyond the reasoning model itself: trained verifiers, multi-paradigm solver selection, or external knowledge bases. The external machinery is effective but imposes practical costs in training data, integration complexity, and domain-specific engineering.

These results raise a direct question: can the reasoning model itself extract useful formal constraints from its own traces, and if so, under what conditions? Same-model self-extraction would require no training data, no external prover, and no second model. Practitioners could augment any LLM with symbolic verification by adding a single extraction prompt and a satisfiability solver. Yet no prior work has systematically evaluated whether self-extraction produces constraints useful for answer aggregation, or characterized the conditions under which it succeeds or fails. This gap is consequential: the practical value of neuro-symbolic reasoning depends on knowing not just whether symbolic methods can help, but \emph{when}.

We evaluate this question through Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA), a pipeline that prompts a single LLM to extract FOL-style constraints (in practice predominantly ground propositional clauses; \S\ref{sec:constraint-extraction}) from $K$ reasoning traces, deduplicates by syntactic equivalence, and solves a weighted partial MAX-SAT problem via Z3 \citep{demoura2008z3}. The answer best supported by the largest satisfiable constraint subset is selected (Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline}). We test seven models from 7B to 32B parameters, including instruction-tuned, reasoning-specialized, and distilled variants, across four reasoning domains (FOLIO \citep{han2022folio}, ProofWriter \citep{tafjord2021proofwriter}, LogiQA \citep{liu2020logiqa}, StrategyQA \citep{geva2021strategyqa}) with supplementary probes on GSM8K \citep{cobbe2021gsm8k} and AIME 2024, totaling more than 2,100 evaluation instances. Oracle controls on FOLIO ($n=204$) and ProofWriter ($n=600$) replace self-extracted constraints with gold annotations verified by Z3, isolating extraction quality from aggregation effectiveness \citep{press2023compositionality}.

The answer is regime-dependent. In the low-accuracy regime (SC $\leq$ 55\%), SICA provides significant gains: Mistral-7B achieves $+4.90$\,pp on FOLIO ($p = 0.013$, $n = 204$). In the high-accuracy regime (SC $\geq$ 63\%), no condition reaches significance across seven conditions (combined $N = 1{,}875$), with $|\Delta| \leq 3.33$\,pp. Oracle experiments yield a fundamentally different result: $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$), which proves the aggregation mechanism is sound. We characterize this as a \emph{regime-dependent capability trap}: stronger models produce consistent traces with low answer entropy, and self-extracted constraints mirror the majority answer rather than providing independent evidence. Confirmation bias reaches 62.3\% for Qwen2.5-14B vs.\ 31.9\% for Mistral-7B; when SICA overrides SC in the high-accuracy regime, the override is correct only 28.6\% of the time. For Mistral-7B, SICA gains concentrate in high-entropy problems ($+9.6$\,pp, $n = 73$), and the aggregate regime difference arises from the proportion of such problems (35.8\% Mistral vs.\ 10.3\% Qwen). Six remediation strategies spanning prompt engineering, cross-model extraction, generational scaling, and solver augmentation all fail to close the extraction-oracle gap (\S\ref{sec:interventions}). For practitioners, the multi-candidate rate $C_0$ combined with SC accuracy forms a two-dimensional screening criterion that identifies the favorable regime (\S\ref{sec:c0}).

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
\item We identify a regime-dependent capability trap in same-model constraint extraction: SICA effectiveness depends on the model's baseline accuracy. Across seven models and four reasoning domains ($N > 2{,}100$), the trap activates above approximately 60\% SC, where confirmation bias renders constraints non-discriminative. Below this threshold, constraints retain partial independence, enabling significant gains ($+4.90$\,pp, $p = 0.013$). Six remediation strategies confirm the trap is structural (\S\ref{sec:main-results}, \S\ref{sec:interventions}).
\item We introduce oracle controls on two datasets that causally localize the bottleneck: replacing self-extraction with gold annotations yields $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO ($p = 2.0 \times 10^{-7}$) and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter ($p < 0.001$). Even the best self-extraction result captures only 34.5\% of the oracle ceiling (\S\ref{sec:oracle}).
\item We provide entropy-conditioned mechanism evidence: SICA gains concentrate in high-entropy problems ($+9.6$\,pp, $n = 73$ for Mistral-7B), and the aggregate regime effect reflects the proportion of such problems in each model's trace distribution. Confirmation bias (62.3\% vs.\ 31.9\%), override precision (28.6\% vs.\ 70.6\%), and unanimous answer rate (58.8\% vs.\ 18.6\%) quantify the causal path from model accuracy to constraint quality (\S\ref{sec:entropy}).
\item We propose $C_0$ and SC accuracy as a two-dimensional, zero-cost diagnostic: low $C_0$ rules out SICA benefit by construction, while high $C_0$ with high SC identifies the capability trap regime (\S\ref{sec:c0}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluated Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation across seven models from four base architectures (7B to 32B parameters) on four reasoning domains with more than 2,100 total instances. SICA's effectiveness is regime-dependent: in the low-accuracy regime (Self-Consistency $\leq$ 55\%), Mistral-7B achieves $+4.90$\,pp on FOLIO ($p = 0.013$), while above approximately 63\% Self-Consistency, seven conditions produce $|\Delta| \leq 3.33$\,pp, all nonsignificant. Oracle experiments replacing self-extraction with gold annotations yield $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO ($p = 2.0 \times 10^{-7}$) and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter ($p = 9.21 \times 10^{-15}$). This causally localizes the bottleneck to extraction quality: the MAX-SAT aggregation mechanism is sound when supplied with high-quality constraints. Entropy-conditioned analysis reveals the mechanism behind the regime boundary. Stronger models produce consistent traces with low answer entropy, which causes self-extracted constraints to exhibit confirmation bias (62.3\% for Qwen2.5-14B) rather than independent discriminative signal. Override precision drops to 28.6\%, and MAX-SAT degenerates to counting (803/804 agreement with count-only on $n = 804$). For weaker models, traces diverge more frequently: confirmation bias falls to 31.9\% (Mistral-7B), override precision rises to 70.6\%, and SICA provides partial gains.

Six remediation strategies spanning prompt design, model architecture, and solver-level interventions all fail to close the extraction-oracle gap (\S\ref{sec:interventions}). High $C_0$ with high SC ($\geq$ 63\%) activates the capability trap. High $C_0$ with low SC ($\leq$ 55\%) is the favorable regime, though even here self-extraction captures only 34.5\% of the oracle ceiling. The oracle gaps ($+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO, $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter) quantify recoverable potential; trained extractors supervised on gold annotations and external provers that verify constraints independently of the reasoning model remain viable paths to close this gap.
